question: In Britain and its colonies, the day after 2 September 1752 was officially 14 September 1752. Why did eleven days simply disappear from the calendar?
correct_answer: Switch from Julian to Gregorian calendar
alternative_answers: Calendar reform to the Gregorian system
Correcting the Julian calendar's drift against the solar year
Britain caught up with the Gregorian calendar used in Europe
headline_answer: Switch from Julian to Gregorian calendar
source_excerpt: The Act advanced the calendar date by 11 days to realign with the solar year, with 2 September 1752 being followed by 14 September 1752.

extra.verification_notes: The Calendar (New Style) Act 1750 switched Britain and colonies from Julian to Gregorian calendar, skipping 11 days from 2-14 September 1752 to correct accumulated drift.

explanation: Britain adopted the Gregorian calendar with the Calendar (New Style) Act 1750, catching up with most of Catholic Europe, which had switched back in 1582. The older Julian calendar counted every fourth year as a leap year without exception, so it drifted about three days every four centuries against the solar year. By 1752 the gap had grown to eleven days, so Parliament ordered them dropped in one jump: people went to bed on 2 September and woke up on 14 September. The same act also moved the start of the legal year from 25 March to 1 January.

question: Which Greek philosopher was hired by King Philip of Macedon to tutor his teenage son, the future Alexander the Great?
source_excerpt: In 343 BCE, King Philip II of Macedon hired Aristotle to educate his thirteen-year-old son, Alexander.

extra.why_interesting: Players know both names but rarely connect them; the greatest philosopher of antiquity spent years as a schoolteacher to the future conqueror of Persia.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple authoritative sources confirm Philip II of Macedon hired Aristotle in 343 BCE to tutor the teenage Alexander.

explanation: Aristotle taught Alexander for about three years from the age of thirteen, and Aristotle had himself been a pupil of Plato, so the chain runs Socrates to Plato to Aristotle to Alexander.

question: How many years did Nelson Mandela spend in prison before his release in 1990?
source_excerpt: Nelson Mandela ... was released from prison after 27 years on February 11, 1990.

extra.why_interesting: Most players know it was 'a very long time'; the exact figure, and the fact he became president only four years later, makes the number land.
extra.verification_notes: Mandela was released on 11 February 1990 after 27 years in prison, a well-documented and undisputed historical fact.

explanation: He was jailed in 1962 and spent most of those years on Robben Island, then walked out in 1990 and was elected president of South Africa just four years later.

question: Marie Curie is the only person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Which two?
source_excerpt: Marie Curie is the only person to have won a Nobel Prize in two different sciences, physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911.

extra.why_interesting: Players know she won twice; naming the two fields makes them realise she was not simply 'the radioactivity scientist' but crossed disciplines.
extra.verification_notes: Marie Curie remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911); no one has repeated this since.

explanation: She shared the 1903 Physics prize for research on radioactivity, then won the 1911 Chemistry prize on her own for discovering polonium and radium.

question: Which British prime minister won the Nobel Prize in Literature?
source_excerpt: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1953 was awarded to Winston Churchill "for his mastery of historical and biographical description..."

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a wartime leader would get a Peace Prize if anything; the Literature prize for a sitting prime minister is the surprise.
extra.verification_notes: Winston Churchill, who served as British Prime Minister, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953 for his historical/biographical writing and oratory.

explanation: He won it in 1953 for his historical writing and speeches, while he was serving his second term in Downing Street.

question: Which scientist, famous for his laws of motion, spent the last three decades of his life running England's Royal Mint and personally hunting down counterfeiters?
source_excerpt: Isaac Newton, Warden and Master of the Royal Mint 1696-1727

extra.why_interesting: The stern figure of gravity and calculus is hard to picture as a detective prowling London taverns, yet that is how he spent his final decades.
extra.verification_notes: Newton served as Warden (1696) then Master (1699) of the Royal Mint until his death in 1727 — roughly the last three decades of his life — and personally investigated/prosecuted counterfeiters like William Chaloner.

explanation: Newton became Warden of the Mint in 1696, went undercover in taverns to gather evidence, and sent the notorious forger William Chaloner to the gallows.

question: In 1952, which world-famous physicist was offered the presidency of Israel and politely turned it down?
source_excerpt: he had neither the natural ability nor the experience to deal properly with people and to exercise official functions

extra.why_interesting: Players think of Einstein as purely a scientist; the idea that he could have been a head of state, and turned it down, is a genuine jolt.
extra.verification_notes: Confirmed: after President Chaim Weizmann's death in 1952, Einstein was offered Israel's presidency and declined, saying he lacked the aptitude and experience.

explanation: The offer came from Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion after the first president died, and Einstein replied that he lacked the aptitude for dealing with people and official functions.

question: Mansa Musa, often called the richest man who ever lived, ruled which West African empire in the fourteenth century?
source_excerpt: Mansa Musa was the ninth Mansa of the Mali Empire, which reached its territorial peak during his reign.

extra.why_interesting: Players may have heard 'richest man ever' but usually cannot place him on the map; the answer relocates medieval wealth away from Europe.
extra.verification_notes: Mansa Musa ruled the Mali Empire c. 1312–1337, matching the question and answer.

explanation: His 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca gave away so much gold along the way that the metal's price in Cairo reportedly slumped for years afterwards.

question: Which future Roman leader, kidnapped by pirates as a young man, reportedly complained that his ransom was set too low, then had his captors crucified once he was freed?
source_excerpt: he laughed at them for not knowing who it was they had captured and suggested that 50 talents would be a more appropriate amount

extra.why_interesting: The audacity of demanding a higher ransom for yourself is so on-brand that players who hear the story can deduce the man from the personality.
extra.verification_notes: Well-documented anecdote confirmed by Plutarch and modern historians: Caesar insisted his pirate captors raise the ransom from 20 to 50 talents, then after release raised a fleet and had them crucified.

explanation: Plutarch says the pirates asked for twenty talents and Caesar insisted on fifty, then raised ships after his release, captured the pirates and had them executed as he had promised.

question: The video-game company Nintendo was founded in which decade?

extra.why_interesting: Players anchor Nintendo to the 1980s console boom; learning it predates the automobile age reframes the company entirely.
extra.verification_notes: Nintendo was founded on September 23, 1889 in Kyoto (as a playing-card company, later becoming a video-game company), confirming the 1880s answer.

explanation: Nintendo started in Kyoto in 1889 making hanafuda playing cards, and did not release a video game until roughly eighty years later.

question: True or false: Christopher Columbus set foot on the mainland of what is now the United States.
source_excerpt: Columbus never set foot on the mainland of North America, let alone the United States.

extra.why_interesting: The 'Columbus discovered America' shorthand makes most players assume he landed in what is now the USA; he never did.
extra.verification_notes: Columbus's four voyages reached the Caribbean, Central America, and Venezuela's coast, but he never set foot on the North American mainland now part of the US.

explanation: Across four voyages he landed in the Bahamas, the Caribbean islands and the coasts of Central and South America, but never the North American mainland.

question: Which former US president, campaigning for a return to office in 1912, was shot in the chest in Milwaukee and insisted on delivering his speech before going to hospital?
source_excerpt: Roosevelt insisted on delivering his scheduled speech ... before allowing himself to be taken to the hospital

extra.why_interesting: Players know him as the rugged Rough Rider; the stem's footholds of 1912 and 'former president running again' let a thoughtful player reach him.
extra.verification_notes: Confirmed: Theodore Roosevelt, running for president again in 1912 after previously serving 1901–1909, was shot in Milwaukee on Oct 14, 1912, and delivered his speech before seeking medical care.

explanation: The bullet was slowed by his folded fifty-page speech and a steel glasses case in his pocket, and he spoke for about ninety minutes with blood spreading across his shirt.

question: France last used the guillotine to execute a prisoner in which year?
source_excerpt: Djandoubi was the last person to be executed by guillotine, both in France and in the Western world.

extra.why_interesting: Players file the guillotine under the French Revolution; discovering it was still in use in the era of Star Wars and punk rock is a shock.
extra.verification_notes: Hamida Djandoubi was guillotined on 10 September 1977 in Marseille, the last execution by guillotine in France, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Hamida Djandoubi was guillotined in Marseille in September 1977, the same year Star Wars came out, and France abolished the death penalty four years later.

question: Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address came straight after a two-hour oration by Edward Everett. Roughly how long did Lincoln's own speech take to deliver?
source_excerpt: Lincoln's address, some 273 words in length, was over in a couple of minutes.

extra.why_interesting: The most famous speech in American history is assumed to be a lengthy address; the two-hour opener in the stem gives a foothold to guess how tiny it really was.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple authoritative sources confirm Lincoln's speech lasted roughly two to three minutes, and Everett himself famously wrote he wished he'd come as near the 'central idea' in two hours as Lincoln did in two minutes.

explanation: The address is only around 270 words long, and by some accounts the photographer had not finished setting up before Lincoln sat back down.

question: As a young man, which future Roman ruler was kidnapped by pirates and, insulted by the ransom they demanded, insisted they more than double it because he was worth far more?
source_excerpt: Caesar found the ransom demand of 20 talents insulting and told them to ask for 50 instead.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a kidnapping victim begs for a lower price; here the captive haggled his own ransom upward out of sheer arrogance, and the name behind it is one everyone knows.
extra.verification_notes: Well-documented ancient anecdote (per Plutarch/Suetonius) confirmed by Britannica: young Caesar, captured by Cilician pirates, demanded they raise his ransom from 20 to 50 talents.

explanation: The pirates duly got their higher ransom, but once freed Caesar raised ships, hunted them down and had every one of them crucified.
